content: Sambucus nigra, commonly known as elder or elderberry, is a species of elder native to most parts of Europe, northwest Africa, and southwest Asia. It is also referred to as black elder, European elder, European elderberry, European black elderberry, common elder, or elder bush when differentiation from other Sambucus species is necessary. This plant thrives in a variety of environmental conditions, including both wet and dry soils, and it prefers sunny locations. It is a deciduous shrub that typically grows to a height of 4 to 6 meters, though it can occasionally reach up to 10 meters. The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs and measure 10 to 30 cm in length. They are pinnate, consisting of five to seven (rarely nine) leaflets, each 5 to 12 cm long and 3 to 5 cm wide, with serrated edges. The flowers of Sambucus nigra are hermaphroditic and bloom in large corymbs measuring 10 to 25 cm in diameter during mid-summer. Each individual flower is white, approximately 5 to 6 mm in diameter, and has five petals. These flowers are primarily pollinated by flies. The fruit is a dark purple to black berry, 3 to 5 mm in diameter, which grows in drooping clusters during late autumn. These berries serve as an important food source for many fruit-eating birds, particularly blackcaps. There are several closely related species of Sambucus native to Asia and North America, which are very similar to Sambucus nigra. Some botanists classify these as subspecies of Sambucus nigra. Uses Sambucus nigra has both medicinal and ornamental applications. However, it is also considered a poisonous plant for mammals and is sometimes classified as a weed. The flower heads are commonly used to make infusions, which are popular as refreshing beverages in Northern Europe and the Balkans. These are commercially available as elderflower cordial and similar products. The berries are edible but only after cooking. All other parts of the plant are toxic, as they contain harmful calcium oxalate crystals. Historically, the strong-smelling foliage was tied to a horse's mane to repel flies during riding. Extracts from the stem bark, leaves, flowers, fruits, and roots have been used in traditional medicine to treat bronchitis, cough, upper respiratory tract infections, and fever. In Beerse, Belgium, the berries are used to produce a type of Jenever called Beers Vlierke.
